rows.verified: The Yellow Card scheme helps MHRA monitor the safety of healthcare products used in the UK.
Suspected adverse reactions can be reported for medicines, vaccines, blood products, immunoglobulins, herbal medicines and homeopathic remedies.
Medical-device incidents involving products available on the UK market can be reported through the scheme.
The scheme also accepts reports about defective and suspected counterfeit medicines or medical devices.
Patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals and healthcare students can submit reports, and only a suspicion is needed.
Serious or medically significant suspected reactions and reactions involving black-triangle medicines should be reported.
Reports may cover suspected reactions associated with medication errors, misuse, overdose, unlicensed use or off-label use.
Useful reports include medical history, concomitant medicines, onset timing, treatment dates and information about effects after treatment stopped.
A Yellow Card report is a safety signal whose interpretation depends on clinical history, exposure, timing, product use and other possible causes.
Yellow Card evidence is report-, patient-, product-, exposure- and time-specific and does not establish an exact parcel-level risk probability.
A seat belt must normally be worn when one is fitted to the occupied seat.
Only one person may occupy each seat fitted with a seat belt.
Children generally need the correct child seat until reaching 135 centimetres in height or their twelfth birthday, whichever occurs first.
Children aged 12 or 13, and younger children over 135 centimetres, must use a seat belt.
A driver is responsible for ensuring children under 14 use the correct restraint or seat belt.
In most circumstances, a child under 3 must travel in a child car seat.
Special rules apply to taxis, minicabs, minibuses, coaches, vans, unexpected necessary journeys and situations with no room for another child seat.
For an unexpected, necessary, short journey, a child aged 3 or older may use an adult belt when the correct child seat is unavailable.
Restraint suitability depends on the child’s age, height, weight, seat, vehicle, restraint design, installation and permitted exception.
Child-restraint evidence is child-, vehicle-, seat-, journey- and installation-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
